idiom_name: extension methods / given type-class instances plus an instance-keyed side map for state
implementation_notes: Scala attaches interfaces without touching the type: Scala 3 extension syntax - extension (d: Document) def words: List[String] = ... - or a type class with given instances, which the language reference recommends over the deprecated implicit class because it 'integrates better with type classes'. That reference states the pattern's core advantage directly: 'Adding a new interface to a class requires changing the source code of that class. By contrast, instances for type classes can be defined anywhere.' Extension methods resolve statically (the receiver becomes an argument), so behaviour is attached with no changes to the subject and no runtime registry; state has no such mechanism, so the canonical replacement is an external map keyed by the instance (mutable.HashMap, or scala.collection.mutable.WeakHashMap when lifetime follows the key) confined to the object or package that owns the capability, with the capability check exposed as an Option rather than a raw lookup.
code_sketch:
trait SpellChecker[A]:                       // type class: behaviour
  extension (a: A) def words: List[String]
  def misspelled(a: A, dict: Set[String]): List[String] =
    words(a).filterNot(dict)

given SpellChecker[Document] with
  extension (d: Document) def words: List[String] = split(d.text)

private val state = mutable.WeakHashMap[Document, SpellState]()   // state
pitfalls: Availability follows implicit scope: an extension method defined in an object that is not in the implicit scope of the receiver type is not found, which surfaces as 'value words is not a member of Document', and two givens for the same type produce an ambiguity error at the call site rather than a deterministic override.

Extension and implicit-class methods never override real members - a member with the same name always wins - so a library upgrade that adds that member silently changes behaviour at existing call sites.

scala.collection.mutable.WeakHashMap is backed by a Java-style weak map: entries vanish under GC, iteration is unsafe, and it is not thread-safe (concurrent use can corrupt the underlying LinkedHashMap) - it is a cache, not a place to keep attached state that must survive.

Type-class instances are resolved at compile time, so a capability cannot be attached per instance: a given that carries state is effectively a singleton, and per-subject data must go in the side map rather than into the instance.
